name: The Mansion House keeper's household
head: haddock_edward

arrival.note: NOT ATTESTED AND VERY LIKELY EARLIER. Nothing dates Haddock's arrival at Chicago; what is dated is his tenancy of a tavern ending in 1835. A year-precision 1835 value would straddle the scene date, so the earliest year the evidence permits is used and the whole field is graded conjectural. TO RESOLVE: Dexter Graves's household and the marriage that made Haddock his son-in-law would date this properly.

lives_at.note: A landlord lived in his house, and Andreas has him keeping this one until some point in 1835. Both halves are reconstructed.

works_at.note: Derived rather than documented because the tenancy ENDS inside the scene year and the record cannot say on which side of 1 July.

present_on_scene_date.note: THE HONEST ANSWER. Andreas has the house passing to Abram A. Markle at some point in 1835 and gives no month. Haddock may have been keeping the Mansion House on 1 July 1835, or Markle may have been, or Haddock may have left the town. Recorded as uncertain rather than resolved by assumption.

persons.name: Edward H. Haddock

occupation.note: Andreas, printed p. 635: Dexter Graves 'sold it to a Mr. Haddock, his son-in-law, who kept it UNTIL 1835 when it passed into the hands of Abram A. Markle'. So he kept a tavern; whether he was still keeping it on 1 July 1835 is the open half.

persons.note: THE HANDOVER FALLS INSIDE THE SCENE YEAR AND NO SOURCE GIVES A MONTH. On a flat prior a transfer somewhere in 1835 is about as likely to be after 1 July as before it, so this household names Haddock, records Markle in this note, and declines to choose - exactly as data/structures/mansion_house.json does. He was Dexter Graves's son-in-law, which is the only family relation in this parcel that reaches across two households. OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — A DATE OF DEATH, AND NOTHING ABOUT 1835. John Wentworth's roll of old settlers who had died since 1 January 1881, kept for the Calumet Club and printed in the Chicago Tribune of 25 April 1882, carries “Edward H. Haddock, May 30, 1881.”. That corroborates a Chicago residence before 1840 and fixes the END of this life, which this record did not carry; it is not an arrival and it places nobody in the town on 1 July 1835. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Haddock, E. H.” (tax_1833_041, line 93); Poll list of 1835 — “Haddock, E. H.” (poll_1835_028, line 315). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Haddock' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

research_note: THE HOUSEHOLD THAT EXISTS TO CARRY AN UNRESOLVED HANDOVER RATHER THAN TO HIDE IT. The Mansion House had a keeper on 1 July 1835 and this project cannot say which of two named men it was. Writing no household would lose a documented tavern keeper; writing two would double-count a job only one man held; writing Markle would be a coin-flip stated as a fact. So one household is written, graded derived throughout, with presence recorded as uncertain and the alternative named in the notes. A LATER PARCEL SHOULD LOOK FOR THE MONTH - the Chicago American began publishing in June 1835 and a change of landlord is exactly the thing a new paper advertises.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.

address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Haddock, Edward H., commission merchant, South Water st'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: NOT READ BACK, BECAUSE SOMETHING BETTER ALREADY STANDS. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints an address against this name in 1839, and it is left where it is. An 1835 placement already stands: this household works at `mansion_house`, and clause 2 says an attested 1835 placement always beats a door printed 4 years later. The later address stays on the record as 1839's evidence and moves nothing.
